passage: Sit, Abhinav, and I'll tell you about the year I moved to a colony in Nagpur. I was twenty-four, working late at the printing press and coming home at ten. By the second week I heard whispers at the water tap: where does she go so late, why no husband yet? My face burned. I wanted to snap back. Instead I began saying good evening to everyone, and when Mrs. Bhatt was struggling with her shopping, I carried a bag up the stairs. I told her plainly, "I work at the press till nine, and my marriage is my parents' and my own business for now." She said, "Oh." The whispers dried up like a puddle in May. It took two months, mind you. These days the whole colony calls me Vasudha Aunty.

qa.q: Where did Vasudha work when moving to the colony?
qa.a: Vasudha worked late at the printing press.

qa.q: How did Vasudha feel when hearing the whispers at the water tap?
qa.a: Hurt and angry; the burning face and the urge to snap back show it.

qa.q: What choice did Vasudha make instead of snapping back, and what did it change?
qa.a: Vasudha greeted everyone, helped Mrs. Bhatt and spoke plainly about work, and the whispers slowly dried up.

qa.q: How might Mrs. Bhatt have seen Vasudha after the bag and the plain words?
qa.a: As a helpful, honest neighbour rather than a mystery; the surprised Oh suggests a rethink.

grounding: A young person hears neighbours gossip about late hours and marriage and answers with a steady, polite, open manner.

passage: Rain had flooded two roads, so Aditi reached the colony gate at eleven, soaked, with Lakshmi from the office dropping her in an auto. A power cut had left the compound dark, and under the stairwell three neighbours stood around a candle, whispering. Aditi caught "always so late" and "who is this girl every night?" Her ears went warm. She wanted to hurry past. Instead she stopped and said, "Good evening, aunty. This is my colleague Lakshmi. The roads were flooded near the bus stand. Would you like my torch for the stairs?" One neighbour took it, looking embarrassed. Lakshmi grinned as they climbed. "That worked better than a fight, no?"

qa.q: Why did Aditi reach the gate at eleven?
qa.a: Rain had flooded two roads.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling when overhearing the whispers?
qa.a: Embarrassed and stung; her ears went warm and she wanted to hurry past.

qa.q: Which choice turned the moment, and why?
qa.a: Stopping to explain openly and offering the torch showed nothing to hide and gave the gossip little to feed on.

qa.q: How might the neighbour who took the torch have felt?
qa.a: Embarrassed, maybe a little ashamed, and softened by the kindness.

grounding: A young person overhears neighbours discussing late hours and responds with a steady, polite and open manner.

passage: The Sunday yoga class in the Rose Colony community hall ended, and Aparna was rolling up her mat when she heard it from behind the pillar. "Comes back at midnight, every week. And that boy on the bike, who is he?" "Office, she says. Office till midnight?" Aparna froze. Her friend Trisha, beside her, raised her eyebrows and mouthed, "Want me to say something?" Aparna shook her head, cheeks burning. She walked out past the aunties and said, "Good morning, Sharma aunty, Dolly aunty," as warmly as she could. They went red. The next Sunday she brought a tin of banana bread for the class and mentioned, in passing, that her shift at the call centre ended at eleven and her colleague dropped her home. Dolly aunty asked for the recipe. The whispers about midnight stopped, mostly.

qa.q: When did Aparna's call-centre shift end?
qa.a: It ended at eleven.

qa.q: How did Aparna feel when she overheard the aunties?
qa.a: She felt humiliated and hurt; she froze and her cheeks burned.

qa.q: Why did Aparna's calm greeting work better than a fight?
qa.a: Greeting them warmly and later sharing plain facts left nothing to feed the gossip, whereas an angry reply might have given them a new story.

qa.q: How might Trisha have seen the moment behind the pillar?
qa.a: Trisha was probably indignant on Aparna's behalf and ready to confront the aunties, and may have been surprised by how steady Aparna stayed.

grounding: It illustrates a young person who overhears neighbours gossiping about her late hours and answers with a steady, polite and open manner.

passage:
Dear Yamini,
You'll laugh, but I've become the colony's favourite serial. My mother's friend told her that people are saying I've "chosen someone from outside" and that's why I refused the proposal from Mehra uncle's nephew. Nobody asked me, of course. They just decided.
For two days I wanted to march over and tell them to mind their own business. I even rehearsed it in the shower. Instead I've been doing the opposite, which is harder. I say hello to everyone at the milk booth. When Mehra aunty asked, with that sweet voice, "So, any good news?", I said, "Not yet, aunty, I'll tell you first," and smiled. She didn't know what to do with that.
It still stings, honestly. But the stories get boring when I don't react.
Miss you. Write back.
Ishita

qa.q: What were people saying about Ishita?
qa.a: That Ishita had "chosen someone from outside" and that is why the proposal was refused.

qa.q: How did Ishita feel on first hearing the gossip?
qa.a: Ishita felt stung and angry, wanting to march over and even rehearsing what to say in the shower.

qa.q: What does Ishita's reply to Mehra aunty get right?
qa.a: It stays friendly and gives a light, open answer, so there is no defensiveness for the gossip to feed on.

qa.q: How might Yamini feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Yamini might feel protective and sympathetic, perhaps amused by the milk-booth moments, and glad to be the one Ishita confides in.

grounding: It illustrates a young person who learns neighbours are discussing their marriage plans and chooses a polite, steady manner over defensiveness.

passage: Vikas, you know me, I'm Ayesha, I don't care what people think. Except I did. Last month the neighbour across the corridor told my landlord my friends were "coming and going at all hours." Four friends. Once. It was my birthday. The landlord called me and I felt about twelve years old again, being scolded. My first message to that neighbour was long and furious. I didn't send it. Thank God. Instead, the next evening I knocked with leftover cake and said, "Sorry if we were loud on my birthday. If it ever bothers you, please just tell me directly." She looked surprised, almost embarrassed. She said her husband works early. Fair. Now she waves when she sees me. My landlord hasn't called since. It still irritates me that she went around me. But I'm glad I didn't send that message.

qa.q: What did the neighbour tell the landlord?
qa.a: That Ayesha's friends were "coming and going at all hours."

qa.q: How did Ayesha feel when the landlord called?
qa.a: Ayesha felt scolded and small, like twelve years old again, and then furious enough to write a long angry message.

qa.q: What small step helped Ayesha most?
qa.a: Knocking with leftover cake, apologising for the noise and asking to be told directly turned a rumour into a real conversation.

qa.q: How might the neighbour have felt when Ayesha knocked on her door?
qa.a: She seemed surprised and a little embarrassed, perhaps expecting a fight, and may have felt relieved to explain about her husband's early work.

grounding: It illustrates a young person stung by neighbours' gossip about their friends who responds openly and politely rather than defensively.

passage:
Monday. Harsha came home at eleven after her hospital shift and heard it through the stairwell window: "Every night so late. And that boy on the bike dropping her. God knows what her parents think." It was Lakshmi Aunty from the first floor. Harsha's face burned. She wanted to bang on the door.
Wednesday. Harsha met Lakshmi Aunty at the milk booth. Instead of looking away, she smiled. "Aunty, I'm on night duty in the emergency ward this month. Arjun, the boy on the bike, is my colleague; he lives nearby." Lakshmi Aunty blinked. "Oh. Emergency? That must be tiring."
Saturday. Lakshmi Aunty knocked with a steel box of lemon rice. "For after your duty." Harsha noticed the whispers on the stairs had gone quiet. She never did find out whether Aunty had changed her mind, or just her topic.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi Aunty bring on Saturday?
qa.a: She brought a steel box of lemon rice.

qa.q: What did Harsha feel on Monday when she heard the gossip?
qa.a: Harsha felt angry and humiliated, her face burning with an urge to bang on the door.

qa.q: Why did Harsha's approach at the milk booth work?
qa.a: She stayed polite and open, simply sharing the facts about her shift and her colleague, which left the gossip nothing to feed on.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi Aunty have seen Harsha after the milk booth?
qa.a: Lakshmi Aunty seemed surprised and a little sheepish, then concerned, even bringing lemon rice for after Harsha's duty.

grounding: It illustrates a young person gossiped about by neighbours who responds with a steady, polite and open manner that starves the gossip.
